title: The Kelvin scale and absolute zero
keyIdea: Absolute zero, 0 K or about −273 °C, is the temperature at which particles have the least possible kinetic energy, so nothing can be colder. The Kelvin scale starts there, so it has no negative values. A step of 1 K is the same size as 1 °C: to convert, K = °C + 273 and °C = K − 273. The average kinetic energy of gas particles is proportional to the temperature in kelvin.

kid: Particles in a gas zoom about. Cool the gas and they slow down. Keep cooling, and you reach a point where they cannot slow any more. They have the least energy they can ever have. That point is about −273 °C. We call it absolute zero.

Nothing can be colder than absolute zero. So scientists made a scale that starts there. It is the Kelvin scale, and its unit is the kelvin, K. Absolute zero is 0 K. There are no negative numbers on it.

Each step on the Kelvin scale is the same size as a step of one degree Celsius. Only the zero moves. So add 273 to go from °C to K: water freezes at 0 °C, which is 273 K. Take 273 away to go back: 77 K is −196 °C.

A change stays the same on both scales. If a drink warms by 10 °C, it warms by 10 K. You only add 273 to a reading, never to a change. And to double the energy of gas particles, double the kelvin number, not the Celsius one.
adult: This lesson covers the GCSE Physics particle model in England: absolute zero is −273 °C, temperatures are converted between degrees Celsius and kelvin, and the average kinetic energy of gas particles is proportional to the temperature in kelvin. It also supports NGSS HS-PS3-2 on energy at the particle scale. The exact value is −273.15 °C; GCSE work rounds it to −273.

Key terms: absolute zero, kelvin (K), Celsius (°C), absolute (thermodynamic) temperature, internal energy, kinetic energy of particles and gas pressure. Note that we write 300 K, not 300 °K. A sealed gas at constant volume loses pressure in a straight line as it cools. Extending that line to zero pressure gives −273 °C, which is how absolute zero was first estimated.

Common mistakes: adding 273 to a temperature change, so a rise of 5 °C becomes 278 K; subtracting when going from °C to K; writing negative kelvin; thinking 0 °C means no energy; and doubling the Celsius value to double the particle energy. Heating a gas from 27 °C to 54 °C only raises it from 300 K to 327 K, about 9%.

In the lab the learner cools a gas on a twin °C and K thermometer until the particles reach their least possible motion. They find readings on both scales and convert cards both ways. They extend a pressure line to zero pressure, then set a second box to twice the energy of the first.

familyTip: Look up the coldest temperature ever recorded on Earth, about −89 °C in Antarctica. Convert it to kelvin together by adding 273, which gives about 184 K. Then talk about why the number on the Kelvin scale can never go below 0.

visual.caption: Colder or warmer than the point where water freezes (0 °C = 273 K)? Turn each reading into kelvin first. Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: cool a gas to absolute zero on a twin °C/K thermometer, convert both ways, extend a pressure line to −273 °C, double the energy in kelvin.

choices: The temperature at which particles have the least possible kinetic energy, 0 K
The temperature at which water freezes, 0 °C
The coldest temperature ever measured on Earth
practice.hint: Think about the particles: what is the least they can move?
practice.explain: Absolute zero is 0 K, about −273 °C. Particles have the least possible kinetic energy, so nothing can be colder. Water freezes at 0 °C, which is 273 K.

practice.prompt: A freezer is at {c} °C. What is that in kelvin?
practice.hint: Add 273 to the Celsius reading. Adding 273 to a negative number makes it smaller than 273.

practice.prompt: A gas is at {k} K. What is that in °C?
practice.hint: Take 273 away from the kelvin reading.

practice.prompt: A cup of tea cools by 15 °C. By how much does it cool in kelvin?
practice.hint: Is 15 °C here a reading or a change?
practice.explain: A step of 1 °C equals a step of 1 K, so a change of 15 °C is a change of 15 K. You add 273 to readings, not to changes.

pool.prompt: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. What is that in °C?
pool.hint: Going from K to °C, take 273 away.

pool.prompt: Why does the Kelvin scale have no negative values?
choices: It starts at absolute zero, and nothing can be colder than that
Scientists decided to leave negative numbers out
Negative kelvin temperatures are too cold to measure
pool.explain: 0 K is absolute zero, where particles have the least possible kinetic energy. There is no colder temperature, so there is nothing below 0 K to label.

pool.prompt: A summer day is {c} °C. What is that in kelvin?
Dry ice is at {k} K. What is that in °C?
pool.hint: Subtract 273 from the kelvin reading. The answer will be negative.
pool.explain: °C = K − 273, so {k} − 273 = {=k-273} °C. Dry ice is far below freezing.

pool.prompt: A gas at 27 °C is heated to 54 °C. What happens to the average kinetic energy of its particles?
pool.hint: Turn both readings into kelvin before you compare.
pool.explain: 27 °C = 300 K and 54 °C = 327 K. Average kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin, so it rises by 27/300, about 9%, not 100%.

pool.prompt: A sealed gas loses pressure in a straight line as it cools. Where does the line reach zero pressure?
pool.hint: Zero pressure would mean the particles have stopped hitting the walls.
pool.explain: Extending the line gives zero pressure at about −273 °C, which is 0 K, absolute zero. This is how absolute zero was first estimated.

pool.prompt: A gas is at {k} K. What temperature in kelvin would give its particles twice the average kinetic energy?
pool.hint: Average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature.

pool.prompt: A room warms by 5 °C. By how much does it warm in kelvin?
pool.hint: 1 °C and 1 K are the same size of step.
pool.explain: A change of 5 °C is a change of 5 K. Add 273 only to readings, never to a change.
